sets.title: Personal Organization Habits
sets.scenario_prompt: You have volunteered for a research study at your university about personal organization habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

tasks.question: Thanks for volunteering to help us with this research. Today I'd like to ask you some questions about your personal organization habits. Do you consider yourself to be an organized person? Why or why not?
model_responses: Yes, I consider myself fairly organized, especially with schoolwork. At the beginning of each week, I list my assignments, test dates and personal activities in a digital calendar. Then I divide larger projects into smaller tasks and decide which ones need immediate attention. Every evening, I check the list and prepare the books or materials I will need the next day. This routine saves time in the morning and prevents me from forgetting deadlines. I am not perfectly organized because unexpected tasks sometimes change my plan. However, I leave some free time in my schedule so that I can make adjustments without becoming stressed. Being organized does not mean planning every minute. For me, it means knowing my priorities, keeping important materials in predictable places and having a clear idea of what I should do next.
key_phrases: divide a project into smaller tasks
have a clear sense of priorities

tasks.question: Got it. Now, would you say that your organization habits have changed or stayed the same over time? Why do you think that is?
model_responses: My organization habits have improved significantly over time. When I was younger, teachers and parents reminded me about homework, so I rarely planned independently. After entering high school, I had more subjects, activities and deadlines to manage. I sometimes forgot small assignments or started major projects too late. As a result, I began using a calendar and a weekly task list. I also learned to break difficult assignments into steps, such as researching, outlining, writing and revising. Now I review my schedule every evening and select three priorities for the following day. The main reason for this change is greater responsibility. As students become older, other people provide fewer reminders, while the consequences of missing a deadline become more serious. Developing a simple system has helped me become more independent and use limited study time more efficiently.

tasks.question: Very good. Next question: do you think organizational skills should be taught in schools? Why or why not?
model_responses: I believe organizational skills should be taught in schools for two reasons. First, these skills improve academic performance. Students often struggle not because they lack ability, but because they forget deadlines, underestimate the time required or do not know which task to complete first. Lessons on calendars, priorities and breaking projects into steps could help them work more efficiently. Second, organization prepares students for adult responsibilities. University students and employees must manage appointments, documents and several assignments without constant reminders. For example, a teacher could give students a month-long project and show them how to create weekly milestones and review their progress. These techniques are practical and can be applied to every subject. Therefore, schools should not assume that students naturally know how to organize themselves; they should teach these habits and let students practise them.

tasks.question: Sounds good. And my final question: some people believe that being organized can significantly reduce stress. Do you agree or disagree with this viewpoint? Why?
model_responses: I agree that being organized can significantly reduce stress for two reasons. First, an organized system reduces uncertainty. When assignments, appointments and deadlines are recorded in one place, people do not need to keep worrying that they have forgotten something important. They can focus on the current task instead. Second, planning prevents work from accumulating at the last minute. Dividing a large project into small daily steps makes the workload feel manageable and leaves time to solve unexpected problems. For example, a student who begins a presentation two weeks early can research, make slides and practise on different days. This is much less stressful than completing everything the night before. Organization cannot remove every difficulty, but it gives people greater control over their time. That sense of control helps them remain calm and handle busy periods with more confidence.

sets.title: Digital Device Usage

tasks.question: Thank you for agreeing to participate. I'd like to ask you some questions about your use of digital devices. First, how many hours a day do you typically spend using electronics like smartphones, tablets or computers?
model_responses: I typically spend about six hours a day using digital devices, although the amount varies. On school days, I use a laptop for around three hours to research information, write assignments and attend online lessons. I also spend two or three hours on my phone for messages, music, short videos and practical tasks such as checking transportation. For example, I use a timer when watching videos and keep my phone away while studying for a test. On weekends, my recreational use may increase, but I also try to exercise or meet friends in person. Digital devices are essential to my education and communication, but setting limits prevents them from occupying all of my free time.
key_phrases: spend about six hours a day
prevent devices from taking over free time
stay at school during the week
not be allowed to use personal electronics
rely on textbooks and printed worksheets
use a school computer when necessary

tasks.question: Thank you. What types of activities do you usually do on your digital devices? For example, do you use them for work, entertainment, or socializing?
model_responses: I use digital devices mainly for schoolwork, communication and entertainment. For school, I search for reliable information, write papers, prepare presentations and watch educational videos when a textbook explanation is unclear. I also use a calendar and cloud storage to organize assignments and access files on different devices. For communication, I send messages to classmates about group projects and make video calls with relatives who live far away. During breaks, I listen to music, watch short comedy videos or play a simple game. These activities help me relax, but I try not to begin them before completing important work because a short break can easily become an hour. Overall, my devices serve several purposes rather than only entertainment. They make learning and communication more efficient, while reasonable limits help me maintain time for exercise, sleep and face-to-face interaction.

tasks.question: Interesting. Can you tell me about a time when you needed to take a break from using digital tools? How did it affect you?

By Friday, my eyes felt tired, I had difficulty concentrating and I was becoming impatient with small problems. I decided to take a complete two-hour break after school. I turned off notifications, left my phone at home and walked in a nearby park with a friend. At first, I worried that I might miss an important message, but the feeling disappeared quickly. The fresh air and conversation helped me relax, and I returned home with more energy. I finished my work faster that evening because I could concentrate again. This experience taught me that a deliberate break is not wasted time; it can restore attention and make later device use more productive.

tasks.question: Great. Some people believe that spending too much time on personal technology can negatively impact face-to-face social interactions. Do you agree or disagree with this viewpoint? Why?
model_responses: I agree that excessive personal technology use can harm face-to-face interaction for two reasons. First, phones divide people's attention. If someone repeatedly checks messages during a meal or conversation, the other person may feel ignored. The conversation also becomes fragmented because neither person can respond carefully. Second, excessive screen time can replace opportunities for real interaction. For example, a student who spends every free evening watching short videos may have less time to meet friends, join activities or practise starting conversations. Over time, the student may feel less confident when speaking to people in person. Technology is useful for arranging meetings and maintaining distant relationships, but it should support social life rather than occupy all of it. Putting devices away during shared time and making room for regular in-person activities can help people listen better and build stronger relationships.
